---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Asset-Light Profit Scaling Behind A Moat
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(SUB(GROWTH(SUB(sale, cogs), 1), GROWTH(ppegt, 1))), RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale), 3)))
HYPOTHESIS: Firms that grow gross profit faster than gross plant and already command a durable margin are compounding intangible competitive advantage that requires no incremental physical capital, and the market underprices that scalability.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: Knowledge-Backed Gross Profit Scaling is the archive's strongest joint result (fmb 3.22, alpha 3.2%, t 2.98), and this substitutes the R&D-stock gate — which the critic correctly notes is a documented level anomaly with a large zero mass among non-reporters — for the realized-moat gate that has independently produced joint strength on the short side. The test is whether asset-light profit scaling is priced because of research inputs or because of the intangible output they proxy for, and the swap extends the construct to the majority of firms that never report R&D.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Gross Profit Per Employee Without Plant
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), emp), 1)), RANK(NEG(GROWTH(ppegt, 1))))
HYPOTHESIS: Rising gross profit per employee achieved without expanding physical plant is the fingerprint of organizational and human capital — intangible assets that never enter the balance sheet — and firms displaying it earn abnormal returns as the productivity gain proves durable.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: The archive has proxied intangibles only through R&D spending, goodwill and gross margin, never through labor productivity, even though human and organizational capital is the largest unbooked intangible category for most firms; employment is broadly reported, so this avoids the zero-mass problem that flattens the R&D-gated signals. The interaction is necessary because profit per employee can rise simply through capital substitution, and requiring flat or falling gross plant isolates the intangible source from the mechanization source.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: Capacity Expansion Into Eroding Margins
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent)), RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale), 5))))
HYPOTHESIS: Building capacity is most destructive when the firm's competitive position is actively deteriorating, so a multi-year downward margin trajectory identifies over-expansion far better than a low but stable margin level, which may simply reflect a structurally thin-margin business model.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: Capacity Expansion Without Pricing Power is the archive's best short-side joint result, but its level-based gate necessarily confounds industry cost structure with moat erosion, and the critic flagged that it may re-express the gross-profitability anomaly. Replacing the moat level with the moat trajectory isolates that specific design choice while making the economic claim sharper: it is losing pricing power, not having thin margins, that turns investment into value destruction.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 4---
NAME: Research Decay With Capacity Ramp
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(xrd, MA(xrd, 5)))), RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent)))
HYPOTHESIS: An innovator whose current research spending has fallen well below its own five-year norm while it accelerates physical investment is harvesting a depleting knowledge stock, and the market continues to price the firm on an innovation profile it no longer sustains.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: Every R&D leg in the archive is either a cross-sectional level or a one-year change, both of which conflate structural non-innovators with genuine retrenchers; normalizing current R&D by the firm's own five-year average makes the measure scale-free, orthogonal to the published R&D-intensity anomaly, and interpretable only within the innovator population where the depletion story applies. The capacity ramp supplies the reallocation evidence, distinguishing a firm cutting research because it is dying from one deliberately shifting its capital toward replicable hard assets.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 5---
NAME: Acquisitions Without Profit Delivery
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(COALESCE(aqc, 0), 3), at)), RANK(NEG(GROWTH(SUB(sale, cogs), 1))))
HYPOTHESIS: Acquisition spending per se is not the problem; the destructive cases are acquirers whose gross profit fails to grow after the deals, revealing that the purchased revenue carried no incremental rent.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: The acquisition family delivers the archive's largest alphas (-4.5% to -5.4%) with essentially zero Fama-MacBeth slopes, which says the effect lives in a narrow corner rather than along a cross-sectional gradient; conditioning on realized profit delivery rather than on the absence of R&D or margin should concentrate the same corner on economically failing deals while giving the sort a continuous second dimension. If the slope remains flat under this conditioning, we learn that the acquisition alpha is a discrete event effect and further specification search in that family should stop.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 6---
NAME: Brand Capital Versus Capacity Share
EXPRESSION: RATIO(TS_SUM(COALESCE(xad, 0), 3), ADD(TS_SUM(capx, 3), TS_SUM(COALESCE(xad, 0), 3)))
HYPOTHESIS: Firms that devote a larger share of their three-year investment budget to advertising rather than physical capacity are building demand-side intangible capital that is expensed rather than capitalized, and this understated asset base earns a return premium.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: Advertising is the one intangible input in the resource menu the archive has never tested, and it captures a distinct economic channel from research: brand capital protects price rather than product, which is why it may connect to the margin-based moat evidence that has been the archive's most productive conditioning variable. Horizons are matched at three years on both legs and the denominator is strictly positive, avoiding both the horizon-mismatch and small-denominator defects that flagged earlier mix ratios, and the level formulation avoids the spurious jumps that a differenced advertising measure would inject when reporting starts or stops.
INTERACTION_TYPE: ratio

---CRITIQUE Asset-Light Profit Scaling Behind A Moat---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: This is a one-leg swap on the archive's Knowledge-Backed Gross Profit Scaling that recombines two legs already present in the archive (asset-light gross-profit growth and the 3-year gross-margin MA gate), and the substituted gate is essentially the documented gross-profitability/margin level effect, so the incremental learning is narrow even though the construction and sign are internally coherent.

---CRITIQUE Gross Profit Per Employee Without Plant---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 4
RATIONALE: Labor-productivity growth as an unbooked-human-capital proxy is a genuinely new channel for this archive and the expression matches the hypothesis and sign, though be aware the second leg alone is close to the asset-growth/investment anomaly (partly absorbed by CMA in FF5) and emp is coarsely reported.

---CRITIQUE Capacity Expansion Into Eroding Margins---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 4
RATIONALE: Swapping the margin level for a five-year margin trend is a substantive, well-motivated design change that separates structurally thin-margin businesses from firms actually losing pricing power, and the expression's direction matches the stated negative sign; the main risk is that the trend leg alone captures known profitability-change/earnings-momentum effects.

---CRITIQUE Research Decay With Capacity Ramp---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 4
RATIONALE: Normalizing R&D by the firm's own five-year average is a genuine within-firm reframing that is distinct from the archive's level and one-year-change R&D legs and orthogonal to the published R&D-intensity anomaly, with a consistent sign; watch for unstable ratios when the historical R&D base is near zero and for the coverage loss from requiring five years of reported xrd.

---CRITIQUE Acquisitions Without Profit Delivery---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: This is the fifth conditional variant in an acquisition family where four different gates (no R&D, low margin, goodwill overhang, buy-vs-build) all produced nearly identical alphas with flat slopes, strongly implying the aqc leg drives everything and a new gate is cosmetic; the gate is also mechanically contaminated since acquisitions themselves inflate consolidated gross profit growth.

---CRITIQUE Brand Capital Versus Capacity Share---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: Advertising intensity is a well-documented published anomaly, and COALESCE(xad,0) collapses the roughly three-quarters of firms that never report advertising to an exact zero, so the ratio becomes largely a reporter/consumer-industry indicator — precisely the zero-mass defect the proposal claims to avoid.

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Improving Productivity Of Knowledge-Inclusive Capital
EXPRESSION: DELTA(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(ppent, ADD(invt, TS_SUM(COALESCE(xrd, 0), 3)))), 1)
HYPOTHESIS: When the capital base is measured correctly — plant plus inventory plus the capitalized research stock that accounting expenses away — an improvement in gross profit per dollar of that true capital signals rising economic productivity that reported returns on assets understate for research-intensive firms.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
INTERACTION_TYPE: ratio
REASONING: Rather than recombining two archive legs, this transfers the one deflator idea that produced the archive's strongest cross-sectional slope (knowledge-inclusive capital, fmb -5.0 when applied to investment) onto an entirely different quantity, profitability, where it has never been tested, and it does so as a change so the sort is not simply the gross-profitability level that RMW already prices. The interaction is intrinsic to the construct: for a plant-heavy firm the denominator is almost all tangible and the measure reduces to conventional capital productivity, while for a research-heavy firm the expensed knowledge stock dominates and the measure re-prices the firm on capital the balance sheet never recorded.
REASONING: Coverage stays broad because unreported research is genuinely zero capitalized knowledge and the denominator is strictly positive for any operating firm.

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Irreversible Capacity Under Demand Uncertainty
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(VOL(GROWTH(sale, 1), 5)), RANK(RATIO(capx, ADD(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0)))))
HYPOTHESIS: Physical capacity is irreversible while research spending can be throttled year to year, so firms facing volatile demand that nevertheless commit their investment budget to hard assets are exercising real options badly and earn lower subsequent returns.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional
REASONING: The critic is right that the acquisition family is saturated — four different gates produced nearly identical alphas with flat slopes, which is evidence the aqc leg alone drives it — so this slot moves to an untested channel: the irreversibility-versus-flexibility distinction between tangible and intangible investment, which is the deepest economic difference between the two themes and one the archive has never exploited. The interaction is indispensable, since a hard-asset investment mix is perfectly sensible under stable demand and only becomes a real-options error when demand volatility is high.
REASONING: Both legs are broadly measurable and the mix ratio is bounded in the unit interval with a strictly positive denominator whenever the firm invests at all.

---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: Peer-Relative Inventory Build Without Peer-Relative Moat
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(IND_ZSCORE(SUB(GROWTH(invt, 1), GROWTH(sale, 1)))), RANK(NEG(IND_ZSCORE(MA(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale), 3)))))
HYPOTHESIS: Excess inventory accumulation signals value destruction when the firm's pricing power is weak relative to its own industry peers, because a below-peer margin identifies a genuine competitive deficit rather than the structurally thin margins that characterize entire distribution-heavy sectors.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional
REASONING: This abandons advertising entirely, accepting the critic's point that COALESCE(xad, 0) turns the measure into a consumer-industry reporting indicator, and redirects the slot to repairing a specific documented divergence: Inventory Build Without Pricing Power delivered alpha -4.9% with t -4.18 but a Fama-MacBeth slope of only -0.44, exactly the pattern expected if the sort is largely a stable sector tilt that a portfolio spread monetizes but a cross-sectional slope cannot detect. Industry-neutralizing both legs converts the signal from a sector bet into a within-peer-group competitive-position measure, so if the slope becomes significant while the alpha survives, we learn the moat mechanism is real at the firm level rather than an industry artifact.
